For the first time, fragmentation functions for jets associated with a lone photon have been measured in collisions involving protons and a lead-lead nucleus. This analysis utilizes data from the CMS detector at the CERN LHC, considering collisions that occurred at a center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV. The fragmentation functions for jets with masses ranging between 60 and 120 GeV are observed, and are compared to those from proton-proton collisions as well as proton-lead collisions. In central proton-lead collisions, jets appear to be suppressed to an extent slightly greater than what would be expected based on area scaling principles. Moving towards more central proton-lead collisions, this suppression is seen to be suppressed to an extent that exceeds that of proton-proton collisions. Furthermore, jet fragmentation in proton-lead collisions is observed to be softer than what would be expected based on proton-proton collisions. Research indicates that photon-tagged jets that are in the medium's mid-radius are significantly impacted by photons, resulting in considerable medium modification.

Recent research involving Feynman integrals has highlighted the significance of Apéry-type inverse binomial series. Building upon previous findings that non-alternating central binomial series could be solved using level four multiple zeta values, we now show that alternating versions require level eight and can be solved using an alternative approach. This involves the substitution of hyperbolic trigonometric 1-forms for their standard trigonometric counterparts.

Following a recent discovery of potential young Y dwarfs in the Pleiades, an analysis of the data, combined with observations from the Subaru Telescope's 8.2m main dome, has been conducted. This study, therefore, reports the results of follow-up observations, including Pleiades field stars and two of the detected Y candidates, observed using Subaru/HiCIAO at 11.3, 12.8, and 14.1 micrometers. The analysis of these additional data points at higher wavelengths has shown that candidate #2, initially found to have a distinct index at 10.95 micrometers, actually exhibits the the presence of a water absorption feature from 12 to 14 micrometers. However, the initial conclusion that this object may be a young Y dwarf has been ruled out. Meanwhile, candidate #3, which showed significant differences in 10.95 micrometer index, as well as 8.7 and 10.3 micrometers, actually displays 11.3, 12.8, and 14, micrometers features indicative of water absorption, thus pointing to a color pattern consistent with a late T-dwarf. The discovery of pleiades 127T, which has been found to have an estimated age of 120 million years, is noteworthy as it is one of the oldest objects with the current Y-d

The top 10 largest ALICE experiments in terms of particle production for different systems and energy ranges have revealed an intriguing observation: a well-established relationship between radial flow and multiplicity of charged particles. This set of measurements provides a comprehensive and varied view of radial flow and multiplicity of charged particles across diverse systems and energy ranges, including Pb-Pb collisions at 2.76 and 0.524 TeV, p-Pb collisions at 8.3 TeV and at a 6.02 TeV equivalent in collider mode, and also in fixed target mode at 15.8 and 40.0 GeV. Moreover, these experiments studied proton-proton collisions at 7 and 2.76 TeV as well as in collisions with light nuclei such as with $^3$He and with $^{129}$Xe.

We develop a novel, numerically efficient approach to solving DGLAP equations for single and double parton distribution functions by leveraging Chebyshev interpolation techniques. This method enhances numerical precision with a reduced number of grid points for PDF evolution, achieving improved efficiency. The DPD evolution process utilizes a cost-effective grid-point scheme, enabling the incorporation of two distinct renormalization scales for each parton. The proposed methods account for PT-RES contributions across all orders in PDG renormalization and factorization scales, with two-parton evolution at different PT-RES scales explored and analyzed.

Speculative missions to Mars and the Moon have proposed using 3D printing with a raw material known as regolith to rapidly construct habitats. This has led to various 3D printing methods being studied, such as those involving laser sintering and sunlight sintering, which rely on temperature to sinter the print material. Since no suitable binder was found in experiments, it is believed that temperature sintering must be employed to achieve sufficient structural integrity in regolith. This study aimed to investigate the sintering process by subjecting samples of Martian and Lunar soil to various temperatures to analyze their mechanical properties under compression, up to 1 MPa. The results showed that both Martian and Lunar regolith samples reached a peak compressive strength at temperatures between 600-800 C, which is temperature at which they can support stresses up to their expected gravitational loads. This suggests that they can be used as a binding agent without an additional binder to achieve structural integrity in regolith-based construction, such as 3D printed structures on the Moon and Mars, using laser or sunlight to sinter the regolith.

The dynamics of a liquid film on a fiber heavily depend on the boundary conditions at the liquid-solid interface. This understanding has led to a theoretical model that uses the Navier-Stokes equations in a cylindrical coordinate system to examine the effect of liquid-solid slip on a film's stability. The resulting linear analysis shows that perturbation growth rates increase with slip, and this trend accelerates as the Reynolds number increases. Furthermore, the ultimate growth rate is directly linked to the liquid-solid slip coefficient's four power. It has been determined that including slip in analyses provides more comprehensive insights into filament growth compared to its absence.

By comparing star formation rates (SFRs) derived from H$\alpha$ and Brackett-$\beta$ (Br$\beta$) rates in a sample of nearby galaxies, we found significant discrepancies that cannot be explained solely by dust extinction. Our analysis of 11 galaxies with sufficient signal-to-noise ratios for Br$\alpha$ and Br$\beta$ reveals that H$\alpha$/H$\gamma$ is more suppressed than Br$\alpha$ and similarly, H$\alpha$ is more suppressed than Br$\beta$. This pattern is consistent with theoretical predictions, suggesting that recombination radiation is produced closer to its ionizing source in low-density regions and is thus less affected by dust. This research highlights the Br$\alpha$ and Br$\beta$ lines as reliable tracers for measuring SFRs in galaxies and potentially serves as an indicator of non-gravitational forces in the galaxy's interstellar medium.

This investigation classifies the local modules within the high-grade Verlinde network, established in our previous research. We've found the braided auto-equivalences that preserve these local modules form a group, the structure of which varies depending on certain parameters. Notably, there are four exceptional cases where the orbifolds CPO(SO(3), (m, 2)) with four distinct values of m exhibit a different behavior, requiring a separate analysis. In these exceptional scenarios, we'll manually determine local modules and braided auto-equivalences for each case. Our findings also reveal the existence of local modules that aren't part of the high-grade Verlinde network in these exceptional cases, even though the network's higher-category auto-equivalences are fully characterized as direct sums of the four identified.

The Fisher-KPP equation, a reaction-diffusion equation, was first introduced by Fisher for modelling allele spread within genetic populations, but also gained applications by Kolmogorov for a broader range of scenarios. Applying an innovative approach for tackling non-linear partial differential equations provides a distinctive approximate solution to the Fisher-KPP equation, which, however, defies initial intuition. Although the solution respects the maximum principle, a breakdown occurs once time surpasses zero, leading to an extremely irregular, non-smooth outcome that contradicts conventional travelling wave approximations commonly utilised in the study of inertial reaction-diffusion equations.

This work addresses the challenge of handwritten mathematical term classification. A unique mathematical notation system was developed to streamline handwritten mathematical input, and a two-stage approach was implemented to process handwritten equations. A binary classifier was created to distinguish between written and non-written mathematical notation, and a character-level classifier was designed to transcribe individual characters based on the output from the written equation segmentation. A comprehensive dataset was compiled to train and evaluate the proposed system.

This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modeling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a model to directly output phone durations from a speech corpus. We replace the conventional mean with median duration output in order to better capture non-Gaussian duration distributions, including multiple modulations. To achieve this, we modify the regression loss function to minimize the median absolute error instead of mean absolute error. This model can be combined with a phone classification model that outputs either fixed or variable targets, resulting in two variants: PhD-M Median and PhMV-M Median. We compare these models with the established PhD-M and PhMV-M models using a phone error rate and a quality metric called Mean Opinions About Quality. We demonstrate that the median-based models improve speech quality over their mean-based counterparts without requiring changes to other synthesis components.

Species dispersal and migration patterns are critical to understanding species distribution and biodiversity, and variations in species distribution can be attributed to factors such as habitat loss, environmental changes, and historical events like the ice age. To analyze changes in species distribution, researchers utilize General Linear Models (GLM) and Nonlinear Regression models, but these methods can yield biased estimation results if habitat suitability maps contain spatial inaccuracies. This research addresses the problem of spatial inaccuracy in predicting species distribution by proposing an innovative two-step approach that accounts for and corrects errors in species distribution estimates. In the first step, the compounding errors from GLM and Nonlinear Regression models are estimated through Bayesian inference, utilizing an informative prior derived from the posterior distribution of species distribution models. In the second step, the model estimates the corrected distribution by adjusting for the calculated error, using a Nonlinear Regression model. The validity of this approach was verified through simulations, using three real-world bird species in the US, revealed that failing to account for space inaccuracies can significantly underestimate or overestimate species distribution, and the proposed approach offers a reliable estimation of species distribution by correcting estimation biases.

Due to a combination of diverse learning styles and controlled working conditions, the integration of human input enhances the accuracy of interactive deep learning systems in addressing complex medical challenges, such as skin cancer diagnosis.  Although standard deep learning models achieve notable success in skin lesion classification, collaborative deep learning has received relatively little attention in this area.  To bridge this gap, we present the first investigation of cooperative deep learning for identifying malignant skin images.  We compare standard deep learning methods with interactive deep learning methods allowing one, two, or three human annotators to enhance the model's output by refining or modifying predicted skin lesion classifications.  To evaluate the effectiveness of cooperative learning, we focus on two important types of skin cancer using a widely accepted benchmark database consisting of patient-derived images.  We find that cooperative learning enhances the work of base machine learning models by an average of 8% for accurate classification and demonstrates a significant performance boost compared to existing interactive machine learning approaches.  Our discovered insights into interactive machine learning systems provide opportunities for improving medical decision-making support and other complex computer vision applications.

To capture the intrinsic diversity of Type Ia supernovae from their spectral evolution, we employ a probabilistic autoencoder with a physically-meaningful structure to learn a low-dimensional representation from nine preprocessed spectral datasets collected between 2004 and 2018. By using the Nixie physics-informed variational autoencoder with an inverse model, with the help of synthetic spectra, we prevent the learned low-dimensional latent space from being influenced by observational noise. We find that this approach consistently produces spatially distinct and distinct groups in the latent space, which are significantly different from the results of a standard probabilistic autoencoder. The pAE's ability to produce and analyze synthetic supernovae in the training dataset leads to a statistically-distributed and morphologically-representative collection of synthetic spectra, which helps to quantify the uncertainty in spectral data and informs future observational strategies. By analyzing the pAE's output, with the aid of the SIMBA code, we identify a population of "super-Chadwick" supernovae, characterized by strong metallic emission and minimal hydrogen-blue absorption, which are predicted to be produced by the merger of white dwarfs and main-sequence stars. The discovery of these unique events using the pAE's encoded data also confirms their absence in the SN Ia population, providing valuable insights into the nature of Type Ia supernovae.

A massive neutral gas outflow has been identified in a massive star-forming galaxy. The outflow is associated with a massive starburst event. The galaxy, known as HATLASJ085358.9+015537, is among the most luminous star-forming galaxies during the epoch of reionization. The outflow was detected using the ALMA for the CO (1-0) emission line, which was at a redshift of 0.659. The outflow has a mass of 3.3 billion solar masses and is moving at a speed of 360-480 km/s relative to the rest frame of the galaxy. The mass rate of gas loss due to the outflow is approximately 100 solar masses per year. The outflow is consistent with being launched from a region that is approximately 1000 parsecs in size and is confined within an angle of approximately 45 degrees. The gas density within the outflow is approximately 0.3 solar masses per cubic parsec, which is similar to the interstellar medium in the galaxy. The gas outflow is likely to be a result of a massive starburst event that is powering a superwind that is escaping the galaxy. This study explores the dynamics of a steady, continuous plume on an axisymmetric platform, enriched with suspended particles and fluid currents, and further complexified by additional fluid currents and inorganic material. Researchers have measured the plume's growth and the distribution of particles and fluids within it, and found that the presence of inorganic material significantly impacts plume development, its internal composition, and particle distribution. Notably, the distribution of particles and fluids differs, with the plume containing fluid currents, and a distinct boundary between particle-enriched and particle-poor regions. Furthermore, the study reveals that the direction in which particles and fluids enter the plume has a substantial effect on its development and the concentration of particles within, where a downward flux of particles results in higher particle concentrations near the plume's core, and unique boundaries between regions with particle buoyancy fluxes of opposite signs.

Understanding the spread of diseases within networks, such as contact graphs, reveals patterns of disease propagation. However, these graphs often overlook crucial details like the contexts in which individuals come into contact, leading to an incomplete understanding of disease spread. By incorporating hyperedges that represent multiple individuals in the same setting, a more comprehensive model emerges. This approach is guided by the concept of "syndemics," which emphasizes the interconnectedness of health issues and social determinants. By analyzing data from a university campus, we found that adding individual interactions to the model only marginally improved its long-term predictive capabilities, but it became essential for accurately modeling the early stages of disease spread, especially when R_0 is close to one. This insight provides a data-driven basis for how to effectively model epidemics on complex networks, taking individuals' immediate environments into consideration.

Recently, it was discovered that two-dimensional CrI$_3$ exhibits distinct magnetic properties which are influenced by layer thickness and crystal structure. We employ a general model that considers the relationship between magnetic and electronic properties in layered CrI$_3$ to investigate its layer-dependent magnetic behavior. The study reveals the origin of spin canting, observes a first-order transition from an antiferromagnetic to a ferromagnetic state as layers increase, and finds that the transition is influenced by competing magnetic interactions and crystal structure. Additionally, strain can also induce this transformation and even create stable antiferromagnetic states through buckling. Our findings offer a comprehensive explanation for experimentally observed magnetic properties and open up the possibility of tuning the magnetic properties of CrI$_3$ via strain.

Dynamical simulations of solar-type stars reveal the dynamics of stellar rotation, magnetic field generation, and convective flows, all influenced by a key parameter known as the Rossby number. Our three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic models explore turbulent convective flows in rotating stellar interiors, where differences in rotation speed lead to varying levels of global rotation and magnetic field effects. In slowly rotating stars, where the Rossby number is low, simulation outcomes align with established stellar patterns, featuring distinct rotation profiles driven by rotation, convection, and magnetic forces. However, in slowly rotating stars, magnetic energy shows an unexpected increase at higher magnetic numbers, which contradicts expected trends. Further investigation into these results shows that rotational support plays a crucial role in explaining this anomaly. In contrast, rapidly rotating stars, where the Rossby number is high, magnetic forces dominate over global rotation, leading to magnetic energy anisotropy and a-geometry, which are consistent with recent observations of exoplanet host stars. Rapid rotation also gives rise to a dynamo with a dynamo number greater than 10^16, which is necessary for magnetic field amplification. Our studies of solar-type stars reveal that varying the Rossby number yields distinct rotational patterns, magnetic field strengths, and magnetic topology, highlighting the significant impact of stellar rotation on these phenomena.

Deep multimodal learning through integration demands that models process and fuse multiple input forms. This paper introduces the K-fan deep architecture, an elegant model capable of handling multimodal inputs. Notably, the K-fan fan-in fan-out structure facilitates parameter sharing across modalities without increasing complex computations. Furthermore, the K-fan deep model enables cross-modality parameter sharing and flexible modality omission. Experimental outcomes confirm that this model rivals or outperforms other methods on various tasks, including classification, prediction, and estimation.

The use of model checking as a method for verifying the correctness of concurrent programs has been extensively studied, particularly in regards to detecting and preventing deadlocks and data races. Traditional unit tests and functional tests are limited in their ability to capture the subtleties of multi-threaded execution due to their focus on pre-defined test cases. Even model checking, while more comprehensive, may overlook issues arising from unmodeled behavior. To bridge this gap, we propose an approach that leverages model checking and a technique called fuzzing, which generates and modifies test cases dynamically. Our method, called fuzzing for concurrent programs, takes a thread exploration model created from a program model and progressively explores its concurrent executions by introducing and finding new test cases. We have implemented this technique and used it to discover novel data races in several well-known thread exploration models used in prior research.

The widespread use of WhatsApp for information dissemination in recent times has been instrumental in shaping the manner in which misinformation is shared. Although public platforms like Facebook and Twitter facilitate信息共享, the closed nature of WhatsApp enables a rapid and efficient spread of false information among individuals who share it. This is particularly noticeable in regions like India, where users predominantly share links, often from public sources, with their connections and receive unlinked versions of the content, making verification challenging. Although a few studies have attempted to track misinformation on Twitter, a comprehensive understanding of its spread on WhatsApp remains elusive. This research introduces a novel approach to visualize the interplay between Twitter and WhatsApp, highlighting an individual's influence on both platforms. By tracking misinformation sharing on WhatsApp and cross-referencing it with Twitter data, our study's findings reveal that an average of 12% of highly active Twitter followers also engage in sharing misinformation on WhatsApp, with some influencers reaching up to 2000 followers on Twitter and 300 groups (equating to approximately 75000 followers) on WhatsApp.

We analyze a branching population where each individual's offspring distribution depends on the population's frequency spectrum (a category system). A condition is established that ensures a frequent category will persist. This requirement is expressed as an inequality involving the category's frequency and its expected offspring. Notably, this situation bears resemblance to the Malthusian model. A condition is also developed, representing the maximum allowable expected offspring rate for a frequent category, thus preventing unbounded growth. This illustrates that even with a frequent category, unbounded population expansion may not occur. A condition is identified for ensuring that frequent categories will eventually dominate, with our results encompassing and generalizing earlier work.

The primary goal of our spoofing countermeasure system is to achieve high levels of accuracy in verifying user identity across a broad range of attack methods, which utilize various techniques to mimic human responses, without requiring system updates in response to novel attacks. This system is composed of two key modules - an adaptive noise enhancement (ANE) module that isolates authentic user characteristics from template matching, and an attention-based rectified linear unit (AReLU) module that emphasizes sparsity and weak correlations in decision-making. The AReLU module's performance is enhanced by its capability to dynamically select important features and filter out irrelevant information. Extensive testing on the UT Dallas database has demonstrated the effectiveness of this system in achieving a Equal Error Rate (EER) of 1.11% against Attack Type 1, and notably, since the UT Dallas database was not used during the system's training, our results suggest the system's capacity for domain generalization. Furthermore, our experiments reveal that this system's performance improvements on UT Dallas are corroborated by comparable EERs of 1.37% and 1.53% achieved on the Speaker Verification and Anti-Spoofing (SAS) database against Attack Type 2 and 3, respectively, which indicates that this system's performance is somewhat generalizable across different domains.

Supergravity, an extension of special relativity, is a prime candidate for unifying fundamental forces. However, developing inflationary models based on supergravity is complicated by challenges such as non-renormalizability, the problem of cosmological constants, and issues with scalar fields becoming heavy or destabilizing de Sitter vacuums. Despite these challenges, it is possible that supergravity, as an effective low-energy theory, could describe the very early stages of our universe, potentially including the period of cosmic inflation triggered by a complex order parameter from a scalar field or a complex scalar field's infinitesimal transformation. This paper proposes a simple supergravity-based inflation model, examining its couplings to matter fields and evaluating potential issues with scalar fields becoming heavy or destabilizing de Sitter vacuums. Interestingly, this model avoids the trans-Planckian problem, as the scalar field's inflationary excursion is negligible compared to the Planck scale, and it also sidesteps the cosmological constant problem, as the scalar field acquires a mass during inflation, preventing large field excursions post-inflation.

Nonreciprocal optical systems have diverse applications that manipulate the transmission of light based on its propagation direction. This study examines a distinct class of nonreciprocity related to the correlation of photon pairs rather than the transmission of light. An experiment was conducted and supported by theoretical findings, showing this nonreciprocity through second-order coherence functions of photon pairs created by spontaneous four-wave mixing in a silicon microdisk. The study reveals significant differences in coherence functions when the photon pair propagates clockwise versus counter-clockwise.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as leading platforms for quantum computing, yet their effectiveness is hindered by material flaws causing decoherence. A new approach to circuit design incorporates thin films of 11B oxide, a source of 11Be that can be Be-doped into critical components to substitute disorderly atomic impurities. Initial experiments have incorporated 11B into the critical junction regions of superconducting qubits and Josephson resonators and have observed the incorporation effectively increases isotopic composition in these elements. As a direct consequence, Be-doping has been associated with an increase in the lifetime of the qubits. By introducing this innovative method, the performance limitations stemming from manufacturing inconsistencies may be mitigated, thus further improving the effectiveness of superconducting quantum processors.

In 1925, Hausdorff demonstrated that the real line can be divided into specific types of sets, one of which is an uncountable collection of mutually Borel-disjoint sets, each with measure zero and first category. This finding led to questions about how such partitions affect the topological and measure-theoretological properties of these sets when considered as subspaces. Our study provides homeomorphic, Lebesgue-measurable category-preserving and ergodicity results for these partitions, answering a query originally raised by Hausdorff in 1925.

In the 1970s, commodity trading advisors experienced remarkable investment returns. By the 2000s, their track records declined, potentially due to emerging short-term reversal traders who exploit cues provided by CTA prices and returns for profitable trades. Our study examines the interconnection between CTA and stock markets, focusing on how short-term reversal traders' actions impact trading strategies and their decisions based on CTA lags and historical performance, ultimately affecting trading costs and overvalued assets.

Identifying the application protocol in use within a network segment is a crucial task for several key areas, including network security assessment, resource allocation management, and network traffic analysis. Nevertheless, accurately determining the protocol being used can be a complex and challenging task, especially when dealing with encrypted traffic and obfuscated requests that conceal the underlying meaning. To address this issue, our research focuses on developing an innovative, two-stage approach for accurate and meaningful request classification, even when the underlying request is obscured. In the first stage, our system reconstructs the hidden request by integrating an external knowledge graph and then in the second stage, our classification model operates on the graph-enhanced request. With our proposed system, we demonstrate significant improvements in classification accuracy compared to existing state-of-the-art models.

Electrostatic gating allows for controlling the population of particles called magnons, potential future carriers of information, by adjusting their numbers, similar to how semiconductors are doped. A study was conducted using a thin magnetic layer and demonstrated that this control is feasible, showing that magnons can be effectively controlled by electric fields.

A novel approach to federated learning addresses the issue of non-identically distributed data across devices by combining theoretical benefits and practical considerations. This method has the following benefits: it maintains the privacy of user data, handles diverse data distributions across devices, and minimizes communication costs between server and client. The theoretical framework assumes minimally distributed data and employs a two-phase process, where the first phase minimizes local data skew through adaptive sampling, and the second phase ensures convergence of the distributed model. Furthermore, this work presents an efficient aggregation technique to combine models from client devices. The proposed method is supported by convergence rate analysis, which includes results for both stochastic and deterministic settings, along with conditions for unique model convergence. The effectiveness of this approach is validated through experiments on image classification, demonstrating improvements over state-of-the-art methods using the CIFAR-10 dataset.

A comprehensive theoretical model is offered in this paper for analyzing high-dimensional entangled systems, specifically the Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state. Initially, we apply our approach to measure a complete three-photon GHZ state across three dimensions and then extend it to multi-photon systems within higher dimensional settings. In our model, both hyperentanglement of photons and the quantum Fourier transform are employed. The proposed solution will serve as a useful resource for developing high-dimensional quantum computation and communication.

This research examines a multi-user uplink system featuring an intelligent-reflecting-surface that enables the base station to acquire channel information without direct line-of-sight access to user equipment. A comprehensive channel estimation method is developed which leverages linearity and periodicity properties of the channel. This allows us to express a particular linear combination of reflected coefficients in terms of linearity and the discrete Fourier transform with respect to angle-of-arrival at the IRS. This approach substantially reduces the need for pilot symbols, which is critical in scenarios with steep channel spectra. To address the non-convex nature of the associated optimization problem, an alternating minimization-based algorithm is devised, initially tackling special cases before addressing the general case. This method is further enhanced with a probabilistic-separation-based approach to generalize its applicability. Simulations demonstrate that this method of acquisition outperforms existing techniques in various practical scenarios.

This study analyzes data from online news articles to track the evolution of public discourse surrounding the COVID-19 disease in Pennsylvania from March to October 2020. By employing a sophisticated natural language processing technique, we extracted thousands of documents from PennState's campus news network and categorized them based on recurring themes. Subsequently, we utilized a combination of these studies to track how different aspects of the pandemic were covered over time. Our research reveals that initial coverage primarily focused on President Trump's downplaying of the virus, but shifted to emphasize how local officials were prioritizing public health over the economy. Furthermore, we examine the various topics that emerged in the news as a result of the pandemic, such as the use of face masks, protests against racial injustice, and the implications of lockdowns on the economy.

This study investigates the process of being taught to count utilizing a simulated agent and a set of randomly constructed blocks. By analyzing the performance trajectories, there's evident indication of the presence of distinct phases and turning points in the learning process. An external knowledge-based criterion is used to identify an inflection point which coincides with the observed data, allowing for further examination of the learning process up to that point. Notably, the research reveals that the target objects required for training were gradually replaced with new objects throughout the study. Additionally, this research provides evidence of structured behavioral patterns in the decision-making processes of both humans and artificial intelligence systems.

Bloom filters offer quick assessment of whether an element belongs to a set, yet they allow false positives, meaning they may incorrectly indicate a non-member as a genuine element of the set. A variant, the cuckoo filter, provides a more efficient space utilization while maintaining comparable performance. This paper introduces "B+ CFs," a novel in-memory Bloom filter type, combining the best aspects of Bloom+ and the cuckoo filter, and demonstrates improved time and space efficiency over existing in-memory Bloom filter variants, including Bloom+ and the cuckoo filter, across various test scenarios, such as high load factors, insertion rates, and time constraints, as validated by experiments using the Facebook dataset.

Several key connections between convex geometry and holomorphic line bundles on smooth projective varieties or K\"ahler manifolds are explored in this article. We focus on the relationship between positive products and mixed volumes, deriving a generalized Schwarz inequality for log-K\"ahler currents. Furthermore, we develop a criterion for almost all log-K\"ahler currents to satisfy the Levy-Lelong-Sibner inequality, which can be interpreted in the context of optimal transport and O'Neil logsplines on K\"ahler manifolds. Lastly, we establish conditions for almost all K\"ahler forms to yield bounded potentials and extend the capacity's monotonicity and subadditivity to more general complete metric spaces of K\"ahler currents.

A new approach aims to derive market trend insights from dynamic price equations, specifically those that describe how future prices converge to optimal values, thereby maximizing trading volume per unit of time. This methodology stands out for its inherent ability to select a suitable time frame, which is automatically identified by analyzing past market activity and determining the state of highest trading efficiency. To facilitate trend analysis, both historical and forecasted price data are considered, with past prices represented by lagging values and forecasted prices represented by advancing values.

This work presents an innovative technique in federated learning that safeguards against malicious attacks while preserving user privacy. A modified version of decentralized stochastic gradient descent is proposed, allowing clients to reach a consensus and agree on a secure model. Specifically, clients transmit their individual model updates, and a decentralized median calculation is used to determine a group consensus, ensuring that the final model reflects the majority opinion of the updates. Our method demonstrates that the decentralized approach converges at a rate of O(1/sqrt(T)) and effectively resists Byzantine attacks, using 50% of the data from each client. Furthermore, privacy is maintained, and we have established a mathematical relationship between the noise and epsilon in the differential privacy context, showing that our method can provide a certain level of privacy with a probability of at least gamma.

We successfully created a autonomous driving AI that excelled in a simulated racing environment by utilizing imitation learning. The AI, developed with unsupervised trajectory clustering and on-orbit observation of expert human behavior, created its own set of rules for task completion. Additionally, we utilized reinforcement learning to refine its policy by optimizing a reward-based criterion. The AI was taught to complete various tasks with different starting points and was capable of adapting to obstacles, such as moving objects. The results showed that this approach was both sample-efficient in terms of training requirements and transferable across different tasks.

Significant progress in deep learning technology has enabled the creation of more convincingly authentic deepfakes, which have sparked interest across multiple sectors due to their vast potential applications, despite raising serious societal and security risks. This chapter examines the advancements and capabilities in deepfake generation, covering synthesis and detection of deepfake media, as well as potential applications and future research directions in this field.

The identification of sub-Neptune exoplanets in various star systems has prompted inquiries into the potential habitability of these planets, particularly the existence of liquid water oceans on their surfaces, which is essential for life. To address this question, we conducted a study focusing on the statistical distribution of massive planets and how they might impact the habitable potential of these smaller planets. Analysis of Kepler sub-Neptune candidates indicates a significant presence of massive planets within 0.1 AU of their stars, potentially stripping away the atmospheres of smaller planets that form further out. Furthermore, we found that tidal migration, another factor that could affect the habitable potential of these planets, is likely for a considerable portion of Kepler sub-Neptune candidates, especially around stars with low mass. Consequently, it is likely that the true habitable potential of sub-Neptune exoplanets is lower than initially estimated due to the influence of both disk-driven and tidal migration, and especially around stars with low mass.

Inspired by the famous Markov model demonstrated by Mackay in 1987, which showed that a binary neural network could learn sequences through a common input signal, it has been long believed that connections within such networks should be symmetrically connected. By employing a simplified model consisting of two layers of binary neurons, we have found a surprising outcome – the network could actually store a sequence effectively even when connecting layers via a non-symmetric connection, contrary to previous assumptions. Notably, we discovered that when many layers are involved, the network still maintains a connection to the previous layer's state, resulting in accurate predictions for the subsequent sequence elements, as evidenced by high mutual information values between consecutive sequence parts. Our findings highlight the importance of binary neuron models that can serve as theoretical benchmarks for understanding more complex neural networks, ultimately shedding new light on the nature of memory in these networks.

This study introduces a pioneering approach to train an OCR system without relying on previously seen text in training images. Our method leverages a prior knowledge of language, enabling the model to infer unrecognized characters based on the prior language distribution. We integrate this language prior through a module that projects the OCR representation into language probability space and apply KL-divergence as a regularization term to preserve the language prior during training. Our proposed model shows significant improvements in character recognition accuracy for training data's scene text and also excels in texts omitted during training when compared to existing OCR models.

A specific type of chaos expansions can effectively analyze differential equations with uncertain factors by approximating random equilibrium states associated with such equations. This study integrates principles from validated calculations to provide precise error assessments alongside findings about chaos expansions representing random equilibrium states. For this purpose, we developed a new method to calculate posterior distributions of random coefficients in validated calculations, which forms the basis of a posteriori estimates. This approach is demonstrated through examples involving random elliptic equations and a system of random ordinary differential equations.

The increasing prevalence of industrial applications such as IoT systems and Industry 4.0 is accompanied by an escalating problem of high-dimensional time series. This is largely due to the growing demands for real-time monitoring and anomaly detection in systems like smart factories. Addressing these requirements is complicated by the lack of readily available, general-purpose tools for handling high-dimensional time series, which are further exacerbated by the need to identify and localize specific dimensions responsible for anomalies. To bridge this gap, this study provides a comprehensive survey of anemic information systems (AIS), focusing on their potential to facilitate the development of efficient AIS for high-dimensional time series.

Recent findings from multiple studies have suggested the presence of large, ancient disk structures within the Milky Way, originating from the accretion of massive galaxies, specifically identified as Gaia-Sausage Enceladus (GSE) and Wukong (LMS-1). Our analysis indicates that GSE and Wukong possessed infall times for disk development of approximately 2.5 billion and 1.8 billion years respectively, contradicting earlier hypotheses that these galaxies' infalls were nearly instantaneous. To better understand this phenomenon, we introduce a theoretical framework revealing that accreted galaxies typically exhibit delayed infall behavior due to their internal stability, specifically given by the relation $t_{\rm disc} \sim Q^{-1} (M_{\rm halos}/M_{\odot})^{1/3} (M_{\rm local}/M_{\odot})^{-1/6}$. This theory suggests that particularly stable and massive galaxies, like GSE and Wukong, would experience significant delays, supporting observations of delayed disk development and the existence of disk features in certain substructure patterns. For low-density accreted halos, our analysis further suggests the presence of extended infall timescales, explaining observed patterns of arc-like features and suggesting a framework for using such observations to uncover hidden substructures within these halos.

Given a profinite group G and an appropriate S[[G]]-module M of M-{\tilde{M}} type, this research introduces a finiteness theorem for the continuous homology H_*(G, M) with respect to the maximal ideal topology of S. If M is also an S{\tilde{G}}-module, it is proven that the homology H_*(H^0(M{\tilde{G}})) via 'M{\tilde{M}}'' type is an E{\infty} term that maps surjectively to H_*(G, M) with topological solidification, leading to conditions under which the homology H_*(G, M) can be described via a converging spectral sequence of type E_2^* = \bigoplus\limits_{p-q=*} H^{*(q)}_{cont}(G_{ab}, M) => H^{*(p)}_{{\tilde{M}}}.

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify areas of model uncertainty and prioritize document sections for improved model accuracy. Our experiments on the InVista invoice reading task demonstrate the effectiveness of Selective Labeling, as it allows us to achieve the same level of accuracy with roughly 30% fewer annotated examples, along with significant improvements of up to 10% in accuracy when applied to a test set composed of real-world document images.

Using a computational model inspired by density functional theory, researchers investigated interactions at interfaces between InAs and EuS in three distinct bonding setups: blunt/blunt, rounded/rounded, and blunt/rounded bonds. Energy calculations revealed the InAs valence band peak lies higher than that of EuS in all scenarios. A analysis of electronic properties using a Bader method showed that Eu atoms near the interface in blunt/rounded configurations exhibit a reduced magnetic moment compared to those in the bulk. Magnetic properties were also examined and showed that both majority and minority spin electrons experience compression in the presence of InAs. Finally, researchers found that interface strain caused by lattice mismatch does not significantly affect the magnetic behavior within the system.

A comprehensive classification system for subsets of Baire space, categorized by Borel Wadge classes, has been introduced with enhanced effectiveness. Based on Montalbán's true stage machinery, we leverage this innovation to offer an alternative demonstration of Louveau and Saint-Raymond's separation theorem. This leads to a demonstration of Borel Wadge determinacy within the $\text{ATR}_0+\Pi^1_1$-I system of second-order arithmetic.

Deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) have gained significant popularity due to their exceptional performance in visual recognition. However, their training is hindered by several significant drawbacks, including extensive computational requirements, the need for large memory allocation, and the slow speed. While GANs have been proposed to accelerate training, their complex theory and challenging implementation pose additional obstacles. ClickTrain, a novel and practical approach, trains a DCNN by clicking on a single image rather than capturing numerous negative samples, thereby significantly reducing computational requirements and memory allocation while maintaining or even surpassing the accuracy of its GAN-based counterparts.

This research examines the properties of specific modal logics derived from noncommutative lattices by incorporating $\Box$ and $\Diamond$. A particular logic derived from linear ordered groups is considered, specifically from those with no intervals isolated from the identity element. By representing this group ordered language within BCK-formulas, our analysis yields an equivalent formulation within Lambek's group variable fragment. Consequently, given a valued model for this language, we are able to construct a corresponding model for the modal logic defined on a lattice with no isolated intervals, thus establishing the strongest possible completeness result for the considered modal logics.

The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have identified three types of merging compact binaries: binary neutron star neutron star, black hole neutron star, and binary black hole mergers. Advances in numerical relativity and modelfitting methodologies enable us to extract information about the final remnant from these signals, providing insights into the mass and spin of the preceding compact binary system, as well as any potential gravitational wave background. This review provides an overview of current techniques used to produce binary merger remnant signals, focusing on multi-frequency waveforms that can offer more accurate information about a system's properties and remnant formation. It also explores novel, low-complexity methods for analyzing these signals, crucial for rapid follow-up with electromagnetic telescopes and future applications in data analysis and cosmology.

A new discovery has been made regarding a gas giant exoplanet, which orbits around a star called TOI-5542. Some initial research suggests that this exoplanet may be the largest known giant exoplanet with an orbital period of less than 10 days. Although there is significant uncertainty surrounding its potential size, its mass is estimated to be between 1.4 and 4.2 times that of Jupiter. Furthermore, analysis of the star, which is similar in mass to the Sun and has a metal content lower than the Sun, reveals interesting characteristics. Observations of this star, which is 4.5 billion years old and located approximately 430 light-years away in the direction of the constellation Ophiuchus, are consistent with it being a nearly perfect solar twin. Additionally, data collected from multiple sources, which includes information about its radial velocity, radial velocity, and the characteristics of its light, show a 3.1 percent variation with a specific pattern, which is unexpected for stars of similar size and brightness.

A markov decision process, especially its constrained variations, serves as a widely utilized framework for operations management problems, which we now analyze from a different perspective, treating it as a data-driven approximation issue for joint distribution estimation. Our investigation begins by defining the problem of finding optimal policies for constrained Markov decision processes given historical data, then addresses the challenges of sample complexity and computational efficiency. Notably, our results show significant improvements over existing methods under specific conditions, where the state and action spaces are relatively small, offering strong guarantees of sample complexity and computational efficiency regardless of the number of constraints or states/actions. Our approach also introduces a computational guarantee directly linked to the minimum cost associated with an dual problem, enabling the discovery of near-optimal policies within predictable computational bounds. Furthermore, our results provide a novel theoretical understanding of the sample complexity and computational efficiency for optimal policies in constrained Markov decision processes, offering improved estimates with regard to constraints and dimensionality of state and action spaces, which represents a substantial advancement over previous estimates.

This research introduces a hand-written mathematical symbol segmentation challenge.
There are numerous complex, handwritten mathematical symbols that current optical character recognition systems find difficult to process.
To overcome this difficulty, potential solutions could be pursued by first identifying and separating these symbols from handwritten mathematical expressions.
No systems are currently in place to accurately segment hand-written mathematical expressions, thus prompting the creation of a new dataset, HandwrittenMUSIG, consisting of colorful handwritten mathematical symbols and their corresponding colorations, extracted from diverse handwritten mathematical expressions and accompanied by corresponding textual labels. It is proposed that HandwrittenMUSIG could be used to train and evaluate coloration-based segmentation models for handwritten mathematical expressions.

A set of superconformal quantum mechanics theories can be applied to study resolved Calabi-Yao and K\"ahler manifolds, derived from A-type singularities in four-dimensional theories. These superconformal theories encode the BPS states of the parent four-dimensional theory through their twisted Dolbeault cohomology, with BPS indices being equivalent to equivariant twisted Dolbeault cohomology classes. A brane-like object within these superconformal quantum mechanics theories, representing BPS states and factorizing the Hilbert space into charged and neutral segments, corresponds to a functional integral over a field that is holomorphic and quasi-bosonic, within a K\"ahler manifold's super-symmetry multiple. This integral can be evaluated semi-classically using the steepest descent method, with semi-classical states being steepest descent surfaces for specific values of the superpotential, and the steelest descent surfaces being rational for specific values of the superpotential, with all cohomology being represented by semi-classical states. Additionally, a proposed string theory duality has been examined using this brane-like object within superconformal quantum mechanics.

We examine the role of network architecture in the dynamics of epidemics using a deterministic approach to compare two models: one based on continuous time and the other on discrete time discrete space. Applying this framework to the Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible model, we analyze how varying scenarios of disease transmission and recovery impact both models. Our numerical analysis reveals that heterogeneous networks significantly influence the final outbreak size and duration, particularly for heterogeneous networks. Additionally, we observe that both continuous and discrete models exhibit similar patterns of disease spread when host populations are homogeneous, but distinct results for heterogeneous populations. These findings suggest that discrete disease dynamics provide more accurate predictions than continuous dynamics in such scenarios.

Actor-critic reinforcement learning is often hindered by several limitations, including suboptimal exploration techniques, inefficient sample usage and a lack of assurance of policy optimality. To overcome these challenges, we introduce the integrated concept of Simulated Annealing Monte Carlo (SAMC) and Simulated Recalculation Monte Carlo (SRMC) into actor-critic reinforcement learning to yield actor-critic methods with enhanced exploration capabilities, improved sample efficiency and Simulated Recassurance of Optimality (SOO). To this end, we developed Simulated Recassurance Monte Carlo Actor-Critic (SRMC-AC) and Simulated Annealing Actor-Critic (SAMC-AC). Specifically, we present SRMC-AC as a general framework encompassing a broad class of actor-critic methods enhanced by Simulated Recassurance of Optimality, while SAMC-AC extends existing actor-critic methods through Simulated Annealing of Action probabilities.

It's common knowledge that any prime number $p\geq5$ can be expressed in the form $6k\pm1$ for some positive integer $k$. Research indicates that this can be refined to6k\pm a^{2n-1}$for a given natural number $a\geq2$ and odd natural number $a\geq2$. However, the precise values of $k$ and $n$ remain to be fully understood, with current findings suggesting $7\leq n\leq13$.

Autonomous navigation is an intricate process that demands adaptable algorithms and robust decision-making capabilities. Current deep learning-based systems, although efficient, often struggle in complex real-world scenarios and can be susceptible to novel challenges due to the limited robustness of their models and training datasets. Moreover, these systems are rarely designed to account for diverse and extreme environmental conditions that may cause typical sensors to malfunction, such as those found in deep space or hazardous areas. This research introduces a novel deep learning-based autonomous navigation framework, incorporating a specialized attention mechanism and multi-modal fusion decision system, capable of processing multiple sensor inputs and adapting to various working modes and covering a broad spectrum of environmental conditions. The framework's design enables it to function even when certain sensor modalities fail, and to combine information from different sources to enhance its robustness. Moreover, it is capable of adapting to new modalities without necessitating any fine-tuning or re-training. The research demonstrates the framework's efficacy through its deployment on a real robot in a variety of challenging environments, including those with diverse lighting conditions and through the simultaneous processing of multiple sensor types and a modified back-propagation-based re-training strategy.

This in-depth review covers recent research on the spectra of neutral bodies in space, encompassing those with initial rocky or icy compositions and others that have formed through a mix of processes or have experienced significant changes over time, -so-called neutral-sloped bodies. Various theories attempting to account for the I-band spectral diversity in neutral-sloped celestial bodies are examined in detail. These constituents -such as regolith with metallic inclusions, crystalline or amorphous silicates, chondrules, and other materials - are explored as potential explanations for neutral-sloped spectra. Each theory is analyzed in light of observations and other data available from space to Earth. We also look at how these constituents -and neutral bodies in general - can be identified through spectral analysis. These methods include regolith disruption, fluorescence induction, and optical and UV photometric variability, -all of which vary in terms of effectiveness for each theory. We also consider the role these neutral-sloped bodies -regardless of origin or material composition - play in other phenomena, such as the presence of space water via hydroxyl and/or ice, and in space electrical activity.

Let $\mathcal{R}_n(q)$ be the ring consisting of $n \times n$ matrices over the finite field $\mathbb{F}_{\mathbb{F}(q)}$ with zero entries above the main diagonal. Consider the left ideal $\mathcal{P}_i(q)$, which consists of matrices over $\mathbb{F}_{\mathbb{F}(q)}$ with zero entries below the $i$-th diagonal line. It is established that $\mathcal{P}_i(q)$ is free with $q^{n-i}$ generators and that all its proper submodules are also free. Additionally, it is found that for each $i$, the number of non-cyclic submodules of $\mathcal{P}_i(q)$ is equal to $q^{(n-i)(n-i-1)/2}$, and the number of submodules of dimension $k$ that are not free in $\mathcal{P}_i(q)$ is given by a sum of terms of the form $\begin{Bmatrix} n-i \\ k \end{Bmatrix} \mathcal{V}_{\mathbb{F}_{q}}(k, n-i-1)$, where $\mathcal{V}_{\mathbb{F}_{q}}(k,m)$ is the Gaussian polynomial and the term $\begin{Bmatrix} n-i \\ k \end{Bmatrix}$ counts the number of partitions of a

In a 1986 paper in J. Symbolic Logic, Pawlikowski demonstrated that under specific conditions regarding Cohen and random reals, certain model properties can be inferred within extensions of those models. This is proven through a complex interaction between forcing techniques and cardinal characteristics, revealing the depth of set-theoretic interactions. The findings reinforce and complement earlier work by Balcar and Pelant from 1982 in the Archive for Mathematical Logic.

A new pessimism-based approach for Bayesian learning in the offline setting is proposed for creating dynamic treatment regimes. By utilizing a regularized empirical risk minimization technique with cross-entropy regularization, this framework ensures well-behaved policy distributions. It allows us to analyze the regret risk and regret regret directly, without depending on the existence of an optimal policy. A novel "regret regret" metric is defined to measure the regret of the learned DTR from various theoretical and practical perspectives. Experimental results using diverse data sets demonstrate the effectiveness of this learning algorithm.

Dualities between subcategories of finitely generated modules over Artin algebras can be established via tilting or cotilting modules. Specifically, when a algebra $\Lambda$ has a tilting module $T$ over $\Lambda$, there exists a equivalent module $Q$ in $D^{b}(\Lambda)$ with $Q^{**}\cong _{\Lambda}^{**}\Lambda$. Furthermore, $Q^{**}\Lambda^{**}$ is a cotilting $\Lambda$-module, and it can be shown that the category of finitely generated $\Lambda$-modules is dual to the category of finitely generated $\Lambda$-modules with respect to $Q$. The purpose of this article is to introduce and study dualities based on tilting or cotilting modules, referred to as Miyashita dualities, and explore the implications for equivalence of categories between finitely generated $\Lambda$-modules and finitely generated $Q$-modules, where $Q$-modules are defined to be those that are absolutely pure over $\Lambda$ and extendable.

A proposed Witting configuration, with a different complexity of 40 rays, could reformulate the Penrose model for spin-3/2 systems based on a dodecahedron's geometry, to study quantum mechanics' nonlocality and contextuality. An alternative setup using 120 states is examined in this work. These states are defined by a Dhage configuration and can be mapped onto a root system related to the Lie algebra $E_8$, allowing for an exploration of compatibility relations. An investigation into contextuality and nonlocality within this new framework is initiated.
